PHNOM PENH, Cambodia (CNN) -- Cambodia has sent a letter to the United Nations Security Council to call attention to its continuing standoff with Thailand over an ancient border temple on disputed land. Cambodian soldiers stand guard near Preah Vihear temple, close to the Thai border. The country is not asking for U.N. intervention, said Information Minister Kheu Kanharith. Rather, the letter that Cambodia's permanent mission in New York submitted to the chairmen of the Security Council and the General Assembly is meant to draw attention to a crisis that entered its sixth day Sunday. The two countries agreed to meet Monday to defuse tensions -- even as each side continued to amass more troops to the site of the Preah Vihear temple. Both Cambodia and Thailand lay claim to the 11th century temple, which sits atop a cliff on Cambodian soil but has its most accessible entrance on the Thai side. The International Court of Justice awarded the temple to Cambodia in 1962. Thailand claims, however, that the 1.8 square mile (4.6 sq. km) area around it was never fully demarcated. Thailand further says that the dispute arose from the fact that the Cambodian government used a map drawn during the French occupation of Cambodia that places both the temple and the surrounding area in that country's territory. Earlier this month, the United Nations approved Cambodia's application to have the temple listed as a World Heritage Site -- places the U.N. says have outstanding universal value. The decision re-ignited tensions, with some in Thailand fearing it will make it difficult for their country to lay claim to disputed land around the temple. Opposition parties in Thailand used the issue to attack the government, which initially backed the heritage listing. A Thai court overturned the pact, prompting the resignation of Thailand's foreign minister, Noppadon Pattama. He had endorsed the application. Cambodia, meanwhile, is preparing for general elections on July 27. And Prime Minister Hun Sen, who has been in power since the mid-1980s, has portrayed the U.N. recognition as a national triumph. The current flare-up began Tuesday, when Cambodian guards briefly detained three Thais who crossed into the area. Once they were let go, the three refused to leave the territory. Cambodia claims Thailand sent troops to retrieve the trio and gradually built up their numbers. Thailand denies the charge, saying its troops are deployed in Thai territory. Each side has asked its troops to withhold fire unless they are fired upon. So far, the only casualty has been a Thai soldier who was injured Tuesday by a landmine -- possibly left over from the time the Khmer Rouge occupied the area. The Khmer Rouge, a radical communist movement that ruled Cambodia from 1975 to 1979, won power through a guerrilla war. It is remembered for the deaths of as many as 1.5 million Cambodians. -- Journalist Soeum Yin contributed to this report .

# Cambodia Alerts UN Security Council Amid Thai Border Dispute

PHNOM PENH, Cambodia (CNN) -- A letter has been dispatched by Cambodia to the United Nations Security Council, aiming to spotlight the ongoing tension with Thailand regarding a historic temple situated on contested territory along their shared border.

Information Minister Kheu Kanharith clarified that his nation isn't seeking direct UN involvement in resolving the conflict. Instead, the communication—submitted by Cambodia's permanent mission in New York to both the Security Council chairman and the General Assembly president—serves primarily to highlight a standoff that reached its sixth day this past Sunday.

Despite both nations agreeing to hold discussions on Monday aimed at cooling the situation, military buildup continued on both sides near the Preah Vihear temple grounds throughout the negotiations.

At the heart of the dispute lies this 11th-century structure, perched on a cliff technically within Cambodian borders yet more easily reached from the Thai side. While the International Court of Justice granted Cambodia ownership of the temple back in 1962, Thailand contends that the surrounding 1.8-square-mile (4.6 sq km) zone was never properly mapped out. Bangkok further argues that the entire conflict stems from Cambodia's reliance on colonial-era French maps that place both the structure and adjacent land within Cambodian jurisdiction.

Tensions escalated after the UN granted Cambodia's request earlier this month to designate the temple as a World Heritage Site—a status reserved for locations deemed to hold exceptional universal significance. This decision sparked renewed friction, as many Thais worried it could undermine their country's ability to contest ownership of the surrounding disputed zone.

Thailand's opposition parties seized upon this development to criticize the ruling government, which had originally supported the heritage application. A Thai court subsequently struck down the agreement, leading to the resignation of Foreign Minister Noppadon Pattama, who had championed the original bid.

Meanwhile, Cambodia is gearing up for national elections scheduled for July 27, with longtime leader Hun Sen—in power since the mid-1980s—framing the UN's heritage designation as a significant national achievement.

The immediate crisis traces back to Tuesday, when Cambodian border guards briefly held three Thai nationals who had crossed into the contested area. Although released, the trio refused to depart from the territory. According to Cambodian officials, Thailand subsequently dispatched soldiers to retrieve these individuals, with troop numbers gradually increasing afterward. Thai authorities reject this characterization, maintaining their forces remain stationed within Thailand's own borders.

Both governments have instructed their military personnel to hold fire unless directly attacked. The conflict's sole casualty thus far involves a Thai soldier wounded Tuesday by a landmine explosion—potentially a remnant from the era when Khmer Rouge forces controlled the region.

The Khmer Rouge—an extremist communist faction that governed Cambodia from 1975 through 1979 after seizing control through guerrilla warfare—remains infamous for causing the deaths of up to 1.5 million Cambodian citizens.

-- Journalist Soeum Yin contributed to this report.

# Phnom Penh: The Heart of Cambodia

Phnom Penh, the capital and largest city of Cambodia, sits at the confluence of three rivers—the Mekong, the Tonlé Sap, and the Bassac. This strategic location has made the city a vital center of trade, culture, and politics for centuries, ever since it became the permanent capital in 1866 during the reign of King Norodom.

The city's name derives from a legend about a woman named Penh who discovered four Buddha statues floating in the Mekong River. She built a small hill (phnom) and a temple to house them, giving rise to the city's name, which translates to "Hill of Penh." This origin story is commemorated at Wat Phnom, a hilltop pagoda that remains one of the city's most iconic religious sites.

Phnom Penh's history reflects the broader story of Cambodia itself—one marked by both grandeur and profound tragedy. During the French colonial period, the city was transformed with wide boulevards, elegant villas, and architectural landmarks that blended French colonial style with traditional Khmer design. The Royal Palace, with its shimmering Silver Pagoda, stands as a testament to this era and to Cambodia's enduring monarchy.

The darkest chapter in the city's modern history came during the Khmer Rouge regime (1975-1979), when Phnom Penh was forcibly evacuated and much of its population was sent to labor camps in the countryside. The Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum, once a school turned into a notorious prison, now stands as a somber memorial to this period, alongside the Choeung Ek Killing Fields on the city's outskirts.

Today, Phnom Penh has emerged as a dynamic, rapidly modernizing city. Skyscrapers rise alongside traditional markets like the Central Market and Russian Market, while riverside promenades buzz with restaurants, cafes, and nightlife. The city serves as Cambodia's economic engine, hosting government institutions, international organizations, and a growing business sector.

Despite rapid development, Phnom Penh retains a distinctive charm—a blend of French colonial architecture, Buddhist temples, bustling street life, and warm hospitality that continues to draw visitors from around the world. As Cambodia continues its journey of recovery and growth, Phnom Penh remains at the center of the nation's identity and aspirations for the future.

# Tensions Simmer at Preah Vihear as Cambodia, Thailand Trade Accusations Over Ancient Temple

**Border standoff revives decades-old dispute over UNESCO World Heritage site**

Troops remain positioned along a contested stretch of the Cambodia-Thailand border near the ancient Preah Vihear temple this week, as diplomatic tensions escalate over territorial claims that trace back more than a century to French colonial-era maps.

The 11th-century Hindu temple, perched dramatically atop a cliff in the Dangrek Mountains, has once again become the flashpoint for one of Southeast Asia's most persistent territorial disputes—one that has periodically erupted into deadly clashes despite a landmark international ruling meant to settle the matter decades ago.

## A Ruling That Didn't End the Dispute

In 1962, the International Court of Justice in The Hague ruled decisively that the Preah Vihear temple itself belonged to Cambodia, rejecting Thailand's territorial claims and ordering Thai forces to withdraw from the site. The court based its decision largely on a 1907 map drawn up during the French colonial period, when France administered Cambodia as a protectorate.

Thailand accepted the ruling but never fully embraced it, arguing the map contained inaccuracies and that the surrounding land—roughly 4.6 square kilometers adjacent to the temple—remained disputed territory not explicitly addressed by the court.

That ambiguity has fueled recurring friction for more than 60 years. The dispute flared violently between 2008 and 2011, when Cambodia's successful bid to have Preah Vihear listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site reignited Thai nationalist anger. Sporadic gunfire and artillery exchanges during that period killed at least a dozen soldiers and civilians on both sides and displaced thousands of villagers from border communities.

In 2013, the ICJ issued a clarifying judgment, affirming that the disputed surrounding area also fell under Cambodian sovereignty—a decision Thailand accepted only reluctantly, with many Thai nationalists continuing to view the ruling as unjust.

## Current Standoff

Officials from both nations have reported troop buildups near the disputed frontier in recent days, with Phnom Penh and Bangkok issuing dueling statements accusing each other of provocative movements and violations of previous bilateral agreements governing the border area.

Cambodian officials have called for restraint and adherence to the 2013 ICJ ruling, while Thai military officials have characterized their positioning as defensive measures in response to what they describe as unauthorized Cambodian construction and troop movements in contested zones.

Regional analysts note that domestic political pressures in both countries may be exacerbating the standoff. Nationalist sentiment around border sovereignty remains a potent political tool in both Phnom Penh and Bangkok, complicating efforts at quiet diplomatic resolution.

"This is a dispute that never really goes away—it just goes dormant," said one regional security analyst who has studied the conflict for years. "Any perceived slight, any construction project, any troop rotation can reignite tensions because the underlying nationalist narratives on both sides remain unresolved, even when the legal question has been answered."

## Diplomatic Efforts Underway

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), of which both countries are members, has historically played a limited mediating role, generally favoring bilateral resolution over multilateral intervention. Cambodian and Thai foreign ministry officials are reportedly in contact through established border liaison committees, though no formal talks have been announced publicly.

Local communities on both sides of the frontier, many of whom depend on cross-border trade and tourism tied to the temple complex, have expressed growing anxiety about potential disruptions. Preah Vihear draws thousands of visitors annually, and prolonged military tension threatens both tourism revenue and the fragile normalcy of daily life in border villages.

For now, the ancient stones of Preah Vihear stand as they have for a millennium—silent witnesses to a modern dispute that international law has twice attempted to resolve, but which national pride has repeatedly reignited.

---

**PHNOM PENH** — Military forces from Cambodia and Thailand remained in a tense standoff for a sixth consecutive day near the ancient Preah Vihear temple complex, as diplomatic efforts to defuse the situation showed limited progress amid continued troop buildups on both sides of the disputed border area.

## Current Situation

Soldiers from both nations have maintained close-range positions near the 11th-century Hindu temple, with reports indicating no exchange of fire but persistent friction as commanders on the ground navigate an uneasy proximity. Local villagers in border communities have reportedly faced disruptions to daily life, with some families relocating amid fears that the standoff could escalate.

Military officials from both countries have held periodic talks at the local level aimed at preventing miscalculation, though a comprehensive de-escalation agreement has remained elusive. Regional observers note that supply lines and reinforcements have continued moving toward the area, raising concerns about the potential for an unintended clash.

## Diplomatic Reactions

The standoff has drawn attention from regional and international bodies. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), of which both Cambodia and Thailand are members, has faced calls to mediate, though the organization's principle of non-interference in members' internal affairs has historically limited its role in bilateral disputes of this nature.

Cambodian officials have reiterated their position that the temple and surrounding territory fall under Cambodian sovereignty, pointing to international legal precedent. Thai officials, meanwhile, have emphasized concerns over the demarcation of surrounding land, particularly a 4.6-square-kilometer area that has remained contested despite rulings on the temple itself.

Diplomats from both nations have engaged in back-channel communications, with foreign ministries issuing statements urging restraint while avoiding language that might inflame nationalist sentiment at home. Regional powers, including China, and Western nations with interests in Southeast Asian stability have called for peaceful resolution through bilateral dialogue.

## Historical Context

The dispute over Preah Vihear temple is rooted in colonial-era boundary demarcations dating to the early 20th century, when French colonial authorities administered Cambodia and drew border maps that placed the temple within Cambodian territory. Thailand has periodically contested this boundary, arguing discrepancies in surveying methods used at the time.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled in 1962 that the temple itself belongs to Cambodia, a decision that resolved sovereignty over the structure but left ambiguity regarding the immediate surrounding land. This ambiguity has fueled recurring tensions, including previous standoffs and skirmishes between the two nations' militaries.

The temple, perched dramatically atop the Dangrek mountain range, was granted UNESCO World Heritage status, a designation that Cambodia has viewed as an affirmation of its historical and cultural claims—while Thailand has expressed concern that the listing failed to adequately address the unresolved boundary questions in the vicinity.

## Outlook

As the standoff continues, analysts caution that nationalist pressures within both countries could complicate efforts toward a swift resolution. Calls for a joint boundary commission to resume stalled demarcation work have resurfaced, though previous such initiatives have struggled to produce lasting agreements.

For now, residents near the border and observers in Phnom Penh and Bangkok alike are watching closely, hopeful that continued dialogue—rather than further military escalation—will define the coming days.

# Cambodia Turns to UN Security Council as Preah Vihear Dispute Threatens Regional Stability

**PHNOM PENH** — Cambodia has formally requested an emergency session of the United Nations Security Council, escalating a decades-old border dispute with Thailand into an international crisis that is reshaping domestic politics in both countries.

## The Appeal to the UN

Cambodian officials say the decision to bypass bilateral negotiations and bring the matter directly to the Security Council stemmed from a breakdown in trust following renewed military skirmishes near the 11th-century Preah Vihear temple complex. The ancient Khmer temple, perched dramatically on a clifftop along the Thai-Cambodian border, was awarded to Cambodia by the International Court of Justice in 1962 — a ruling Thailand has never fully accepted in practice, even as it formally recognizes it.

Phnom Penh's foreign ministry argues that repeated exchanges of gunfire, troop buildups, and what it calls Thai incursions into Cambodian territory near the temple represent a threat to regional peace that warrants international intervention rather than continued reliance on fragile bilateral or ASEAN-mediated talks. Cambodia has accused Thailand of using the dispute to project nationalist strength domestically, while Thailand counters that Cambodia has militarized a UNESCO World Heritage listing to entrench its claims over contested adjacent land.

By internationalizing the conflict, Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Sen's government seeks not only a binding resolution but also diplomatic leverage — placing Thailand under the scrutiny of the international community at a moment when Bangkok's own government is politically vulnerable.

## Political Fallout in Thailand

The temple standoff has landed squarely in the middle of Thailand's fractured political landscape. Nationalist factions and the *People's Alliance for Democracy* (PAD), the so-called "Yellow Shirts," seized on the border dispute to accuse the Thai government of ceding sovereignty, using the issue as a rallying cry in their broader campaign against the ruling administration.

Critics argue the government's initial support for Cambodia's UNESCO listing bid in 2008 — seen at the time as a goodwill gesture — was exploited by opposition figures as evidence of weakness and mismanagement of national territory. The resulting backlash contributed to renewed street protests and added pressure on an already unstable coalition government grappling with legitimacy questions in the wake of prior political upheavals.

Thai military leaders, wary of appearing soft on sovereignty issues, have taken a harder line at the border, complicating diplomatic efforts and reflecting the broader civil-military tensions that have long defined Thai politics.

## Cambodia's Domestic Calculus

For Hun Sen, the timing is far from incidental. With national elections looming, the Preah Vihear dispute has become a potent nationalist tool. By positioning himself as the defender of Cambodian sovereignty and Khmer heritage against a historically dominant neighbor, Hun Sen has moved to consolidate support ahead of the vote, sidelining opposition criticism on issues like corruption and governance.

Cambodian state media has amplified coverage of the temple standoff, framing the government's UN appeal as a diplomatic victory and evidence of strong leadership on the world stage. Analysts note that invoking historical grievances against Thailand — a country with a long, complicated history of political and military dominance over Cambodia — resonates deeply with Cambodian voters and helps unify a fractious political base.

## A Fragile Path Forward

With both governments facing domestic pressure to appear uncompromising, diplomats warn that a swift resolution remains unlikely. ASEAN, of which both nations are members, has struggled to mediate effectively, hampered by its principle of non-interference in member states' affairs. The UN Security Council's involvement — while largely symbolic given the body's limited enforcement power over such bilateral territorial disputes — nonetheless signals how deeply intertwined the Preah Vihear conflict has become with the internal political survival of leaders in both Phnom Penh and Bangkok.

As troops remain stationed near the ancient temple grounds, the dispute stands as a stark reminder of how historical grievances, contested borders, and domestic political ambition can converge to destabilize an entire region.

# Tensions Flare Along Cambodia-Thailand Border as Troops Mass Near Ancient Temple

*By CNN Staff*

**PHNOM PENH, Cambodia** — Military tensions have escalated along the disputed Cambodia-Thailand border this week, with both nations reinforcing troop positions near the 11th-century Preah Vihear temple complex, a UNESCO World Heritage site that has been a flashpoint between the two Southeast Asian neighbors for more than a decade.

Cambodian officials say Thai forces have moved additional units into the contested border zone, while Thailand has accused Cambodian soldiers of encroaching on land it claims as sovereign territory. The temple itself sits atop a cliff in the Dangrek Mountains, with its main access route running through Thailand, even though international courts have twice ruled the site belongs to Cambodia.

"We call for calm and dialogue, not confrontation," said a spokesperson for Cambodia's Ministry of National Defense in a briefing Tuesday. "This temple represents the soul of the Khmer people. We will defend our sovereignty, but we do not seek war with our neighbors."

A representative from Cambodia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs echoed that sentiment, telling reporters that Phnom Penh has requested an emergency session with ASEAN mediators. "We have engaged in good faith with international bodies before, including the International Court of Justice, and we will do so again," the official said. "What we cannot accept is unilateral military pressure at a sacred and legally recognized site."

## A Legal History of Dispute

The temple, known as Prasat Preah Vihear in Khmer, was awarded to Cambodia by the International Court of Justice in a landmark 1962 ruling, a decision reaffirmed in 2013 after renewed clashes broke out between 2008 and 2011 that killed dozens of soldiers and civilians on both sides. Despite the rulings, the roughly 1.8 square miles of land surrounding the temple has remained contested, with both governments citing colonial-era maps drawn up by French surveyors as the root of the disagreement.

## The Deadly Legacy of Landmines

Compounding the danger of any renewed conflict is the presence of landmines left over from Cambodia's brutal Khmer Rouge era and the decades of civil war that followed. Between 1975 and 1979, the Khmer Rouge regime, along with Vietnamese forces and various factions during the subsequent occupation and civil conflict through the 1990s, laid millions of mines along Cambodia's borders, particularly in the north and northwest near Thailand.

The border region surrounding Preah Vihear remains one of the most heavily mined areas in the country. The Cambodian Mine Action Centre estimates that unexploded ordnance and landmines still contaminate large swaths of land near the Dangrek range, decades after the fighting that planted them ended.

"Every time tensions rise in this area, we are reminded of a war most of the world has forgotten," said a demining official with the Cambodian Mine Action Centre, who has worked to clear the border region for over a decade. "Soldiers today are not just facing each other — they are walking through fields that still hold the wounds of the Khmer Rouge."

Cambodia remains one of the most landmine-affected countries in the world. Government estimates suggest more than 40,000 Cambodians have lost limbs to landmines and unexploded ordnance since the 1980s, with casualties continuing to occur annually, including among farmers, children, and soldiers stationed near the border.

## Calls for De-escalation

Regional analysts warn that any miscalculation near the temple could reignite the kind of deadly skirmishes seen more than a decade ago. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), of which both Cambodia and Thailand are members, has historically struggled to mediate the dispute, constrained by its principle of non-interference in member states' internal affairs.

Cambodian Prime Minister's office released a statement Wednesday urging "restraint and respect for international law," while calling on Thailand to withdraw what it described as "newly fortified positions" near the temple grounds.

Thai officials have not yet responded publicly to Cambodia's latest statements, though a Thai army spokesperson previously stated that troop movements were "defensive in nature" and aimed at protecting Thai citizens living near the border.

As of Thursday, no casualties had been reported, but residents in nearby Cambodian villages say they have been advised to avoid unfamiliar paths and to report any suspicious metal objects — a grim routine familiar to those who have lived near this border for generations.

*CNN's [correspondents] contributed reporting from the region.*
